title: Offline replay dedupe and epochal ledger reconciliation
creator: Maya Kline
description:
Problem: mobile and intermittently-connected clients occasionally re-upload partially-complete or delayed inference requests. These replays can be submitted via the same session id, a new session id, or through proxy paths that canonicalize differently, and they can vary slightly due to client truncation, different encoding, or local pre-tokenization. The current ledger attributes credits on first-write per session id and timestamp; it misses many replayed requests or double-charges clients when replays arrive under different identifiers.

Objective: build a robust reconciliation pipeline that detects replayed/duplicated inference payloads across time (across 'epochs'), deduplicates them for billing purposes, and issues retroactive credits when appropriate without compromising privacy or introducing race conditions that could undercount legitimate concurrent requests.

Scope: server-side fingerprinting of request content post-tokenization, epochal ledger markers (daily/hourly epochs depending on volume), an offline reconciliation job that performs exact and fuzzy dedupe, retro-crediting workflow, observability and alerts, and SDK guidance for mobile clients to reduce ambiguity.

Design sketch:
- Fingerprint: normalize inputs server-side after tokenization to produce a compact fingerprint: canonicalize whitespace, canonical Unicode normalization, remove ephemeral metadata, then compute sha256 of token id sequence. Store fingerprint alongside ledger entry.
- Epochs: ledgers are sharded into epochs (configurable, default 24h). Each incoming request is recorded with epoch id and fingerprint. First-seen within an epoch is billable; subsequent matches within the same epoch are flagged as duplicates and not billed.
- Cross-epoch reconciliation: periodic batch job compares fingerprints across adjacent epochs within a configurable backfill window (default 7 days) to detect late-arriving duplicates; policy: if fingerprint appears in a prior epoch and the earlier record is unchanged, mark the newer entry as duplicate and enqueue retro-credit.
- Fuzzy matching: for truncated or slightly-altered payloads we run a lightweight fuzzy-match pipeline: Levenshtein distance on normalized token ids and a prefix/subsequence heuristic. Fuzzy matches are scored; above a conservative threshold (e.g., 0.92 similarity) we surface candidates for automated retro-crediting. Lower-confidence matches are routed to an audit queue.
- Privacy: fingerprints are derived from token ids (not raw user text) and salted with a per-tenant KMS-managed salt. Salt rotation is supported; rotation does not invalidate past matches because we store both the raw fingerprint and a tenant-salt-version tag.
- Atomicity: record insertion uses idempotent upserts keyed by (tenant, request_id, epoch) and also inserts a fingerprint index. Reconciliation marks entries with a deterministic 'duplicate_of' pointer to the authoritative first-seen entry to avoid racey credits. Retro-crediting is performed via the existing billing adjustment flow and annotated in the ledger for auditability.

Trade-offs and discussions:
- Client-side vs server-side fingerprinting: client-side can reduce duplicates before upload but risks SDK fragmentation and inconsistent tokenizers. We favor server-side post-tokenization fingerprinting for correctness; SDK guidance will still recommend stable identifiers to reduce churn.
- Exact vs fuzzy match: exact matches are cheap and safe. Fuzzy matches increase false positives; therefore fuzzy auto-crediting threshold is conservative and audit pipeline exists.
- Cost: maintaining extra fingerprint indices increases storage and index cost. We plan a TTL on fingerprint-only entries after reconciliation window to bound growth.

Acceptance criteria:
- End-to-end pipeline detects >= 99% of synthetic replays in the e2e harness (see tests) with false-positive auto-credit rate <= 0.1%.
- Retro-crediting job completes without causing negative balances (safety checks) and logs every action to the audit ledger.
- Dashboard shows duplicate_rate, retro_credit_count, fuzzy_candidates, and reconciliation_lag with alerts on anomalies.
- SDK guidance doc and mobile quickstart updated with best-practices for stable request ids and resumable uploads.

Implementation plan:
1) Minimal fingerprint index and exact-match dedupe (feature flagged) + unit tests (2 weeks).
2) Reconciliation batch job, retro-credit integration, and safety checks (2 weeks).
3) Fuzzy matching prototype and audit queue + QA (2 weeks).
4) Monitoring/dashboards, runbook, and SDK guidance (1 week).
5) Graduation from feature flag with staged rollout to 10% -> 50% -> 100% tenants (1 week).

Metrics & monitoring: duplicate_rate (unique duplicates / total requests), retro_credit_count, reconcile_errors, reconciliation_lag_seconds, fuzzy_auto_credit_rate, audit_queue_size. Dashboard link: https://console.redwood.example.com/dashboards/metering/duplicates (placeholder).

Artifacts: Confluence design: https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/METER/pages/Offline+Replay+Dedupe (draft), GH PR (draft): https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/14267, reconciliation job prototype: https://go.redwood/recon-proto (internal shortcut).

Open questions/TODOs:
- Finalize fuzzy similarity threshold and performance budget; need bench of real-world mobile replays.
- Decide on TTL policy for fingerprint indices after backfill window.
- Confirm KMS salt rotation policy with security team.
- Coordinate with Billing team on retro-credit UX and SLA for corrections.

Risks: overzealous fuzzy auto-crediting could reduce revenue and frustrate downstream chargeback reconciliation; underdetecting duplicates leaves customers overcharged. Auditability and conservative thresholds mitigate both risks.
